 Texas early voting sees strong turnout despite concerns
 BY 
 Barbara Campos 
 Texas 
 PUBLISHED 9:00 AM CT Oct. 22, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 9:00 AM CDT Oct. 22, 2026 
 SHARE 
 TEXAS — More than 700,000 Texans have cast their ballots in the first three days of early voting, according to the Texas Secretary of State’s Office, as election officials across the state report strong turnout and smooth operations despite concerns over a voter registration backlog.
 The backlog, linked to software issues at the Texas Department of Public Safety, raised questions about whether some voters would encounter problems at the polls. In Harris County, the state’s most populous county, election officials say voting has been running smoothly, with more than 200,000 ballots cast so far.
 County officials report no staffing shortages at polling locations, voting discrepancies or unusual increases in provisional ballots.
 Provisional ballots allow voters whose eligibility cannot immediately be confirmed to cast a ballot while election officials review their registration status. So far, those ballots account for less than 1% of votes cast in Harris County.
 Meanwhile, officials in smaller counties say they are still working through registration concerns while managing high voter turnout.
 In Rockwall County, approximately 3,500 voter registration applications were delayed because of the DPS software error.
 “We’re still working through that population of voters, but we have had no interruptions for those people,” said Christopher Lynch, Rockwall County’s elections administrator.
 Despite those challenges, the North Texas county, which is the smallest county in Texas by geographic area, is reporting a historic start to early voting.
 “In the 12 years that I’ve been here, that is the singular, most singular largest turnout on the first day of early voting since I’ve been here,” said Lynch.
 Lynch says processing mail-in ballot applications has kept his five-person team busy, with employees working overtime to keep up with demand.
 “I was looking at a stack of applications that came in the mail between yesterday and today, so those have to be processed, then the whole process of getting the ballot in an envelope and out to that voter, that is a time consuming, labor intense process, so yes it’s a lot,” Lynch said.
 For eligible Texans planning to vote by mail, Friday, Oct. 23, is the deadline to apply for a mail-in ballot. Applications must be received by the early voting clerk by that date, not simply postmarked.
 In-person early voting continues across Texas through Friday, Oct. 30, ahead of Election Day on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
